prurient

/PROOR-ee-uhnt/ - the stress falls on PROOR · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Prurient means showing an excessive, unwholesome interest in indecent matters.

The landlady called her window-watching neighborly concern, but the notebook logging every tenant's visitors suggested something more prurient.

Example

The gallery billed its exhibition as a study of censorship; the visitors who skipped every wall text and crowded straight to the banned photographs made the show's real, prurient appeal hard to deny.

Prurient condemns the appetite, not the material: it describes the itch to peer at indecent things under whatever respectable excuse is handy. Curiosity can be healthy and nosiness merely rude; prurient interest has crossed into the unwholesome.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

voyeuristic: Voyeuristic means peeping at private moments for the thrill of watching unseen. Prurient judges the appetite rather than the method: an excessive, unwholesome interest in the indecent, whatever alibi it wears. A voyeur has to hide to look; a prurient reader can flip magazine pages in broad daylight.

leering: Leering is the look itself — openly eyeing what decency says to look away from, right there on the face. Prurient names the appetite behind such looks: an unwholesome interest in the indecent that can wear a respectable excuse. A leer is visible; prurient interest can pass for concern.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

wholesome: clean-minded and good for you

chaste: pure in thought and conduct

Where it sits · how improper its chosen subject is — curious → nosy → prurient

curious vs. prurient: Curious is far milder than prurient — an open, healthy wanting-to-know.

nosy vs. prurient: Nosy stops short of prurient: the nosy neighbor pries into any business at all, while prurient interest fixes, unwholesomely, on the indecent kind.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — pruri

Root — pruri: to itch, to long for (Latin prurire)

Suffix — -ent

Suffix — -ent: in a state of (adjective ending)

Put it together

Put it together: Pruri- (to itch) + -ent (in a state of) = itching. Latin prurire named a literal itch and, by extension, the itch to see or hear what decency forbids; a prurient interest is one that scratches.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Latin prurire, 'to itch,' left almost nothing else in everyday English — its only other descendant, the medical term pruritus, stays inside dermatology clinics. The itch survives in prurient alone.

Strength Check

Word Choice

formal / disapproving

Prurient always accuses — it says the interest itself is dirty, whatever alibi it wears. Pair it with interest, curiosity, or appeal. Its unit neighbors carve up the territory: profane is offensive language or irreverence, ribald is crude humor, and prurient is the audience's unwholesome itch to look.
